digest.intro: Books shredded for training data, phones wiped at borders, war paused for talks.

items.title: The Iran War Widens on Two Fronts
items.blurb: A two-week US-Iran escalation — triggered by Iran targeting Strait of Hormuz shipping — has now paused for a second straight day as Trump signals room for talks. Meanwhile the week's underreported storyline: a US-Saudi bilateral nuclear deal that effectively mirrors the NPT but in a bilateral frame, creating an enrichment carve-out that Iran, still nominally an NPT signatory, cannot get. That's a structural crack in non-proliferation logic, not just a deal.

items.title: North Korea Prepares Another 30,000 Troops for Russia
items.blurb: Zelenskyy says Russia has been staging the Voronezh region — 289 miles south of Moscow — since June to receive an additional 30,000 DPRK troops, more than double what's currently deployed. Pyongyang is also sending more ballistic missile launchers. Zelenskyy's real warning isn't just about Ukraine: Russia is giving North Korea live-fire combat experience and weapons refinement at scale, which it will carry home.

items.title: AI Companies Are Buying Antique Books, Ingesting Their Contents, and Then Destroying Them at Incredible Scale
items.blurb: Anthropic ran a hydraulic cutting machine to strip pages from used books, scanned them with industrial imagers, then pulped them — exploiting first-sale doctrine so no copyright permission was needed. A judge ruled this "transformative" fair use. Now ISBNdb, which calls itself the world's largest book database, is marketing itself as an AI training data supplier, turning the rare-book market into a pipeline for ingestion-at-scale before the cultural record gets too contaminated with AI-generated text to be useful.

items.title: US Citizen Charged After GrapheneOS Phone Wipes During Airport Search
items.blurb: Sam Tunick returned from the Dominican Republic and was pulled into secondary screening; his GrapheneOS duress PIN triggered, wiping the device. The DOJ is now charging him under 18 USC §2232 — destruction of property to prevent seizure — and the EFF says they've never seen this statute aimed at an operating system feature before. The implication is stark: if your phone is designed to protect you from compelled disclosure, running it may itself become criminal evidence of intent.

items.title: An Inside Look at the Relay Market Powering LLM Token Resellers and Fraud
items.blurb: A shadow market — concentrated in China — has grown up around pooling API keys from abused free trials, hijacked support bots, and stolen credit cards, then reselling LLM access at a discount through open-source proxies like one-api. Buyers get cheap tokens, geo-restriction bypasses, and in some cases training data via distillation. Willison's practical note: there's now a whole ecosystem that profits from finding unprotected endpoints, and LLM vendors still don't offer hard dollar caps on API keys.

items.title: Physically Accurate Black Hole You Can Put in Your Room (WebGL/AR)
items.blurb: Real-time relativistic raymarching running entirely in the browser — gravitational lensing, photon spheres, accretion disk — placed into your actual room via AR. Not a simulation of vibes; the math is the rendering. Worth pulling apart for anyone working at the physical/digital edge in WebGL.

items.title: Decker: A Platform That Builds on the Legacy of HyperCard
items.blurb: Decker is a serious rethinking of HyperCard's card-stack model: 1-bit ditherpunk aesthetic, deep undo, touchscreen support, and a scripting language called Lil that combines Lua's embeddability with APL-family implicit vector arithmetic and a built-in SQL-like query layer. The philosophy is calm computing — software as self-expression, not platform. If you've ever wanted a tool that feels like it was made for you, this is worth an afternoon.

items.title: CABLE 82: Neighborhood Bulletin Boards, circa 1982
items.blurb: Before Nextdoor, before the internet, local cable access channels ran slow-scrolling text bulletin boards with elevator music — hyperlocal community software at its most embryonic, and arguably its most humane. Hans's CABLE 82 project recreates this on a Raspberry Pi with composite output for period-appropriate CRTs, all open-source. It's a clean artifact of what community software looks like when there's no engagement metric, no algorithm, and no one trying to monetize your attention.

facts.fact: Anthropic used a hydraulic cutting machine to physically remove pages from books before scanning them, and a federal judge ruled this 'transformative' fair use — meaning no payment to authors was required.

The US is charging a citizen under a statute normally used for physical evidence destruction — 18 USC §2232 — because a phone feature (the GrapheneOS duress wipe) triggered automatically at a border crossing.

Zelenskyy says Russia has been preparing the Voronezh region — 289 miles south of Moscow — since June specifically to receive 30,000 additional North Korean troops, more than doubling DPRK forces currently in theater.

The LLM token resale market runs on two legitimate open-source API proxy projects — one-api and new-api — repurposed to pool stolen or abused credentials and sell discounted AI access, primarily out of China.

The proposed US-Saudi nuclear deal would grant Saudi Arabia domestic uranium enrichment rights — something even Iran, still an NPT signatory, is not supposed to have — through a bilateral framework rather than the universal treaty.

make_something.prompt: Build a CABLE 82-style bulletin board for a single city block, neighborhood, or friend group — but make it run in a browser, not on TV. Constraint: no accounts, no likes, no replies. Just scrolling text, a timestamp, and one optional image per post. Use the GrapheneOS story as a design principle: what does software look like when it's built to leave no residue? Pair it with Decker's Lil scripting to handle the post queue and you have something worth shipping in a weekend.

art_picks.title: Koyaanisqatsi
art_picks.creator: Godfrey Reggio
art_picks.why: No dialogue, no plot — just Philip Glass's locked grooves under time-lapse footage of systems in motion: infrastructure, bodies, cities breathing. It's less a film than a feedback loop made visible, and it has a way of making you feel the machine you're inside.

art_picks.title: Dragging a Dead Deer Up a Hill
art_picks.creator: Grouper
art_picks.why: Liz Harris buries melody under tape hiss and reverb until the texture becomes the content — music that behaves more like a fog system than a song. Every element is doing structural work while pretending to just be atmosphere.

art_picks.title: Skyspace installations (series)
art_picks.creator: James Turrell
art_picks.why: Turrell's Skyspaces are rooms where the ceiling opens to sky, but the aperture — lit from below — makes real sky look painted, artificial, wrong. It's a precision instrument for interrogating how the brain constructs color and depth from nothing, which hits differently if you spend time thinking about rendering.

events.name: Firelei Báez: feet squelching on wet grass, nourished by uncertainty
events.why: Last week of Báez's first New York show with Hauser & Wirth — a flood of new paintings and bronze ciguapa sculptures where Caribbean folklore, scientific diagrams, and poured paint dissolve into each other; the eight-panel 'View of Nature' alone is worth the trip.

events.name: Made in America: The Industrial Photography of Christopher Payne
events.venue: Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum, 2 East 91st Street, Manhattan
events.why: Seventy-plus large-format photographs of American factories — Eames chairs being born at Herman Miller, flags on rotary screen printers, a room dedicated to tracing raw wool to finished hat — obsessive craft documentation that turns the production floor into something close to sacred geometry.

events.name: MoMA PS1 Warm Up — July 31: Gabber Eleganza, BAE BAE b2b Crystallmess, Cortisa Star, SCRAAATCH
events.venue: MoMA PS1 Courtyard, 22-25 Jackson Ave, Long Island City, Queens
events.why: The July 31 bill — Gabber Eleganza (Italian hardware-heavy post-club), BAE BAE b2b Crystallmess (Afro-diasporic jungle-house), and Baltimore's Cortisa Star — is the most genre-colliding night of the series, and admission includes access to PS1's galleries and Precious Okoyomon's living-forest courtyard installation.

events.name: MoMA PS1 Warm Up — August 7: BADSISTA, Toxe, nguyendowsXP
events.venue: MoMA PS1 Courtyard, 22-25 Jackson Ave, Long Island City, Queens
events.why: São Paulo's BADSISTA and New York/Hanoi's nguyendowsXP make this the most globally-networked night of the run — electronic music built from diasporic fragments and internet-era subcultures, exactly the kind of scene that's still legible as a scene before it hardens into genre.
